# 07 · Comparing Distributions: From CDFs to KL, and the Two Families {.unnumbered}

*A standalone tutorial accompanying W03. One question runs
through it: given two distributions, how far apart are they? The answer is not
unique, and the choices form two families with genuinely different behaviour. We
start where the answer is easiest — one dimension, where you can just compare
CDFs — and find that three familiar quantities are three different norms of the
same gap. Then KL, its relationship to maximum likelihood, and finally the map of
which divergence each family of generative model is actually minimising.*

## 1. In one dimension, compare the CDFs

Two distributions $P$ and $Q$ on $\mathbb{R}$, with CDFs $F$ and $G$. The CDF
determines the distribution completely, so any honest measure of "how different
are $P$ and $Q$" can be read off the gap

$$
\Delta(x) \;=\; F(x) - G(x).
$$

That is a function. To turn a function into a single number you take a norm — and
the three standard choices give three quantities you have already met or are
about to.

$$
\underbrace{\sup_x |\Delta(x)|}_{\textbf{Kolmogorov–Smirnov}}
\qquad
\underbrace{\int |\Delta(x)|\,dx}_{\textbf{Wasserstein-1}}
\qquad
\underbrace{\int \Delta(x)^2\,w(x)\,dx}_{\textbf{Cramér–von Mises}}
$$

The $L^\infty$, $L^1$ and $L^2$ norms of one object. That is the whole taxonomy of
one-dimensional distances-between-CDFs.

### The Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic

$$
D(P,Q) \;=\; \sup_x \big| F(x) - G(x) \big| .
$$

The largest vertical gap between the two CDF curves. It is always in $[0,1]$, it
is a genuine metric, and it is **distribution-free** in a useful sense: if you
replace $P$ by any strictly increasing transformation of itself and do the same to
$Q$, $D$ does not change — because relabelling the axis slides both curves
identically. That invariance is why the KS *test* has a universal critical value
table that does not depend on what you are testing.

Its empirical version is what you would actually compute: replace $F$ by the
empirical CDF $\hat F_n(x) = \frac1n\#\{i : x_i \le x\}$, a staircase with a step
of $1/n$ at each sample, and take the sup — which is attained at one of the data
points, so it is a finite maximum.

For $P = \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and $Q = \mathcal{N}(\mu,1)$ the sup sits at $x=\mu/2$
by symmetry, giving $D = 2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1$: $0.197$ at $\mu = 0.5$, $0.383$ at
$\mu=1$, $0.954$ at $\mu = 4$. Notice how it **saturates** — by $\mu = 4$ it has
nearly exhausted its range and can barely distinguish $\mu = 4$ from $\mu = 40$.

### The $L^1$ norm is a transport cost

Take the same gap and integrate its absolute value instead of maximising it:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \big| F(x) - G(x)\big|\,dx \;=\; W_1(P,Q),
$$

the **Wasserstein-1 distance** — and this is exactly the quantity
[Transport You Can Compute](./09-discrete-transport.qmd) derives as the cheapest
way to move the mass of $P$ onto $Q$ when moving a unit of mass a distance $|x-y|$
costs $|x-y|$. The area between the CDF curves *is* the transport bill.

So the bridge to transport is not an analogy. In one dimension the optimal
transport cost and an $L^1$ norm of the CDF gap are the same number, and the
monotone (quantile) coupling is what achieves it.

Unlike KS, $W_1$ does **not** saturate: for $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ against
$\mathcal{N}(\mu,1)$ it equals exactly $|\mu|$, growing without bound. It answers
"how far?" rather than "how distinguishable?", and that difference will turn out
to matter a great deal in §6.

### And the $L^2$ norm

$\int (F-G)^2 w\,dx$ gives the **Cramér–von Mises** family; with the weight
$w = 1/(G(1-G))$ it is the **Anderson–Darling** statistic, which up-weights the
tails and is correspondingly better at detecting differences out there. These are
goodness-of-fit tools rather than modelling objectives, so we will not use them
further — but they belong on the map.

### Histograms: the same story, discretised

For distributions on a finite ordered set of bins, the integral becomes a sum and
$W_1$ becomes the **Earth Mover's Distance**:
$W_1(p,q) = \sum_k |F_p(k) - F_q(k)|$, which is the discrete transport problem of
[tutorial 09](./09-discrete-transport.qmd) — solvable exactly as a min-cost flow,
with the [Transport Plan Lab](../materials/transport-plan-lab.html){target="_blank"}
to play with.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Where this whole approach stops working

Every construction above needs a **CDF**, and a CDF needs the real line to be
ordered — $F(x) = \mathbb{P}(X \le x)$ has no meaning without $\le$. In
$\mathbb{R}^d$ there is no canonical order, no canonical CDF, and no canonical
"area between the curves".

Transport survives, because a cost $c(x,y)$ makes sense in any dimension — but the
closed form is gone and you are solving an optimisation. What we need instead is a
way to compare distributions **pointwise**, using only the values of the two
densities at the same point and never their order. That is KL.
:::

## 2. KL divergence

For distributions with densities $p$ and $q$,

$$
\boxed{\;\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q) \;=\; \int p(x)\,\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\,dx
\;=\; \mathbb{E}_{x\sim p}\!\left[\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right].\;}
$$

No ordering, no CDF, no dimension limit: it compares the two densities *at each
point*, through their ratio, and averages the log-ratio under $p$.

**It is non-negative**, $\mathrm{KL}(p\|q) \ge 0$ with equality only when
$p = q$ almost everywhere. This is Jensen from
[the inequalities tutorial](./13-inequalities.qmd): $-\log$ is convex, so

$$
\mathrm{KL}(p\|q) = \mathbb{E}_p\!\left[-\log\frac{q}{p}\right]
\;\ge\; -\log \mathbb{E}_p\!\left[\frac{q}{p}\right] = -\log\!\int q = 0 .
$$

**It is not a metric.** It is asymmetric, $\mathrm{KL}(p\|q) \neq \mathrm{KL}(q\|p)$,
and fails the triangle inequality. Hence *divergence*, not distance.

**It is infinite when supports disagree.** If $p(x) > 0$ somewhere $q(x) = 0$, the
integrand is $+\infty$. This is not a technicality — §6 is about the consequences.

**Gaussian closed form**, which is why this course can compute with it:

$$
\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathcal{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)\,\big\|\,\mathcal{N}(\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)\big)
= \log\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1} + \frac{\sigma_1^2 + (\mu_1-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma_2^2} - \frac12 .
$$

With equal variances this collapses to $(\mu_1-\mu_2)^2/2\sigma^2$ — a squared
distance. Every KL term in a diffusion model's training objective is an instance
of this formula, which is the reason the objective reduces to a sum of squared
errors.

## 3. KL is maximum likelihood in disguise

This is the connection that makes KL more than one option among many.

Let $p_{\text{data}}$ be the true distribution and $p_\theta$ your model. Expand:

$$
\mathrm{KL}(p_{\text{data}} \,\|\, p_\theta)
= \underbrace{\int p_{\text{data}}\log p_{\text{data}}}_{-H(p_{\text{data}}),\ \text{no } \theta}
\;-\; \int p_{\text{data}}\log p_\theta .
$$

The first term does not involve $\theta$ at all. So

$$
\arg\min_\theta \mathrm{KL}(p_{\text{data}}\|p_\theta)
= \arg\max_\theta \; \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}}\big[\log p_\theta(x)\big],
$$

and replacing the expectation by its sample average over $x_1,\dots,x_n$ gives

$$
\arg\max_\theta \;\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \log p_\theta(x_i),
$$

which is **exactly the maximum likelihood estimator** of
[Distributions and Maximum Likelihood](./02-distributions-mle.qmd).

::: {.callout-tip}
## The sentence to remember

**Maximum likelihood *is* minimising the forward KL from the data distribution to
the model.** Every time you fit by MLE — the Gaussian fit, logistic regression via
BCE, a normalizing flow — you are minimising $\mathrm{KL}(p_{\text{data}}\|p_\theta)$
whether or not anyone says so. The empirical average is just the Monte Carlo
estimate of an integral you never write down.
:::

### Which way round? Forward and reverse KL behave differently

Because KL is asymmetric, the two directions optimise for different things.

| | $\mathrm{KL}(p_{\text{data}}\|p_\theta)$ — **forward** | $\mathrm{KL}(p_\theta\|p_{\text{data}})$ — **reverse** |
|---|---|---|
| Penalises | $p_\theta$ small where data is | $p_\theta$ large where data is not |
| Behaviour | **mode-covering**: spreads to cover all the data | **mode-seeking**: locks onto one mode |
| Failure mode | blurry averages over modes | ignores modes entirely |
| Used by | maximum likelihood, flows, diffusion bounds | variational inference, the VAE's $q$ |

The forward direction cannot afford $p_\theta \approx 0$ anywhere the data lives —
the log ratio explodes — so it hedges and covers. The reverse direction is
integrated under $p_\theta$, so it simply avoids putting mass in the wrong place
and is content to ignore parts of the target. This is exactly the
single-Gaussian-fitted-to-a-mixture trap of tutorial 02, now with a name.

The gap is not subtle. Fit a single Gaussian to an equal mixture of
$\mathcal{N}(-2, 0.7^2)$ and $\mathcal{N}(2, 0.7^2)$ and the two criteria give
completely different answers, each of which the *other* criterion scores as
terrible:

| Fit | $\mu$ | $\sigma$ | $\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)$ | $\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| forward optimum | $0.00$ | $2.12$ | **0.42** | 0.81 |
| reverse optimum | $\pm1.98$ | $0.73$ | 6.84 | **0.69** |

The forward optimum is exactly **moment matching** — for a Gaussian family,
minimising $\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)$ means matching the mean and variance of $p$, which
is why it lands between the modes where no data lives. The reverse optimum sits
*on* a mode and is the same distance from either, so which one it finds depends
entirely on where the optimiser starts.

**Interactive** — [The KL Lab](../materials/kl-lab.html){target="_blank"} draws
both optima together, shades the two integrands so you can see *where* each
direction pays its penalty, and plots both objectives against $\mu$: forward KL
has a single basin, reverse KL has one per mode with a barrier between them.

<iframe src="../materials/kl-lab.html" width="100%" height="640" style="border: 1px solid #ddd; border-radius: 8px;" loading="lazy" title="Interactive demo: forward and reverse KL fitted to the same bimodal target"></iframe>

## 4. KL is one of a family: the $f$-divergences

Fix a convex $f$ with $f(1) = 0$ and define

$$
D_f(p \,\|\, q) \;=\; \int q(x)\, f\!\left(\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right) dx .
$$

Convexity plus $f(1)=0$ gives $D_f \ge 0$ with equality at $p=q$, by Jensen — the
same one-line argument as for KL. Different $f$, different divergence:

| $f(t)$ | Divergence | Note |
|---|---|---|
| $t\log t$ | $\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)$ | forward KL |
| $-\log t$ | $\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)$ | reverse KL |
| $\tfrac12\lvert t-1\rvert$ | total variation | the only one that is also a metric |
| $(t-1)^2$ | $\chi^2$ | heavy penalty on ratio spikes |
| $(\sqrt t - 1)^2$ | squared Hellinger | bounded, symmetric |
| $t\log\frac{2t}{t+1} + \log\frac{2}{t+1}$ | Jensen–Shannon | symmetric, bounded by $\log 2$ |

All of these share one structural feature, and it is the one that matters: they
depend on $p$ and $q$ **only through the pointwise ratio $p/q$**. They never look
at *where* the points are. Move a lump of $q$'s mass from just beside $p$ to a
mile away and no $f$-divergence notices, because the ratio at every point is
unchanged.

## 5. Wasserstein, and what changes in more than one dimension

So far $W_1$ has appeared only through its one-dimensional formula
$\int |F - G|$. That formula is a happy accident of the line, and it is worth
being precise about what the general object is before relying on it.

**The Kantorovich definition.** For $p \ge 1$ and distributions $P, Q$ on
$\mathbb{R}^d$,

$$
W_p(P,Q) \;=\; \left( \inf_{\gamma \in \Pi(P,Q)}
\int \lVert x - y \rVert^{p} \, d\gamma(x,y) \right)^{1/p},
$$

where $\Pi(P,Q)$ is the set of **couplings** — joint distributions on
$\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d$ whose marginals are $P$ and $Q$. A coupling is
a plan for moving mass; the integral is what the plan costs; $W_p$ is the cost of
the cheapest one. Nothing here mentions densities, which is exactly why it
survives when densities do not exist.

### Why one dimension is special

On the line there is a **total order**, and that changes everything. The optimal
plan is forced to be monotone — cheapest transport never lets paths cross — and
the monotone coupling is unique and explicit. It is the one matching quantile to
quantile, which gives, **for every $p \ge 1$**,

$$
W_p(P,Q) = \left( \int_0^1 \big| F^{-1}(u) - G^{-1}(u) \big|^{p} du \right)^{1/p} .
$$

Sort both samples, subtract, average. $O(n \log n)$, and no optimisation at all.
*(Checked against an exact assignment solver on 3,000-point samples: the sorted
matching reproduces the optimal cost to machine precision at $p = 1, 2, 3$.)*

::: {.callout-warning}
## The CDF formula is $p = 1$ only

The quantile formula above holds for all $p$. The **other** one-dimensional
formula, the one in §1,

$$
W_1(P,Q) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \big| F(x) - G(x) \big| \, dx ,
$$

does not generalise. At $p=1$ the area between the two *CDFs* happens to equal the
area between the two *quantile functions* — the same region, measured along
different axes — so the two expressions agree. For $p > 1$ that coincidence
breaks, and $\big(\int |F-G|^p dx\big)^{1/p}$ is **not** $W_p$ and is not any
Wasserstein distance.

Concretely, for $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ against $\mathcal{N}(1.5, 2^2)$:

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| $\int_0^1 \lvert F^{-1}-G^{-1}\rvert\,du$ | 1.5586 |
| $\int \lvert F-G\rvert\,dx$ | 1.5586 &nbsp;&nbsp;*(agree, as they must at $p=1$)* |
| $W_2 = \big(\int_0^1 \lvert F^{-1}-G^{-1}\rvert^2 du\big)^{1/2}$ | **1.8028** |
| $\big(\int \lvert F-G\rvert^2 dx\big)^{1/2}$ | **0.6918** &nbsp;&nbsp;*(not $W_2$, not anything)* |

When in doubt, work with quantiles: that form is the one that generalises in $p$.
Neither form generalises in **dimension**, which is the subject of the rest of
this section.
:::

For one-dimensional Gaussians the quantile integral collapses to a formula worth
remembering, and it is the $d=1$ case of Bures–Wasserstein below:

$$
W_2\big(\mathcal{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2),\ \mathcal{N}(\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)\big)
= \sqrt{(\mu_1-\mu_2)^2 + (\sigma_1-\sigma_2)^2} .
$$

*(For the pair above: $\sqrt{1.5^2 + 1^2} = 1.8028$, matching the numeric
quantile integral.)*

**In $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $d > 1$ there is no total order**, so this construction
simply has nothing to stand on. There is no quantile function, and no reason a
cheapest plan should be expressible in closed form. What survives is weaker but
still substantial:

- **It is still a linear program.** For empirical measures on $n$ points each, the
  Kantorovich problem is an $n \times n$ assignment problem. Exact solvers cost
  about $O(n^3 \log n)$ — fine for thousands of points, hopeless for millions.
- **The dual still holds.** Kantorovich–Rubinstein gives, for $p = 1$,
  $W_1 = \sup_{\lVert f \rVert_{\mathrm{Lip}} \le 1} \mathbb{E}_P[f] - \mathbb{E}_Q[f]$,
  which is what a WGAN critic estimates.
- **Brenier's theorem replaces the quantile map.** If $P$ is absolutely
  continuous, the optimal $p=2$ plan is *deterministic*: there is a map $T$ with
  $T_\# P = Q$ attaining the infimum, and it is the **gradient of a convex
  function**, $T = \nabla \varphi$. In one dimension "$\nabla\varphi$ with
  $\varphi$ convex" means "increasing", so this is precisely the monotone quantile
  map generalised. Convexity is what replaces the lost total order.

### One case with a closed form: Gaussians

Between $\mathcal{N}(m_1, C_1)$ and $\mathcal{N}(m_2, C_2)$ in any dimension,

$$
\boxed{\;W_2^2 \;=\; \lVert m_1 - m_2 \rVert^2
\;+\; \operatorname{tr}\!\Big( C_1 + C_2 - 2\big(C_2^{1/2} C_1 C_2^{1/2}\big)^{1/2} \Big).\;}
$$

This is the **Bures–Wasserstein** distance. When the covariances commute — in
particular when both are diagonal — the trace term collapses to
$\lVert C_1^{1/2} - C_2^{1/2} \rVert_F^2$, so the means contribute Euclidean
distance and the covariances contribute Frobenius distance between the *square
roots*.

*(Checked numerically: for a 2-D pair the formula gives $2.35331$, and exact
optimal transport between $4{,}000$-point empirical samples gives $2.35356$.)*

This is the formula behind the Fréchet Inception Distance, which is simply
$W_2$ between two Gaussians fitted to network features — accurate only to the
extent that those features really are Gaussian.

### The two costs of using it in high dimension

**Computation** is the visible cost, and it is the one people usually try to fix.
Entropic regularisation adds $\varepsilon H(\gamma)$ to the objective, which makes
it strictly convex and solvable by **Sinkhorn** iterations costing $O(n^2)$ each —
fast and differentiable, at the price of a blurred plan and a biased distance.

**Statistics** is the cost that actually bites. The empirical Wasserstein distance
converges to the truth at rate

$$
\mathbb{E}\,W_p(P_n, P) \;\asymp\; n^{-1/d} \qquad (d > 2p),
$$

which is the curse of dimensionality again, in a new costume. Measured on
independent samples from $\mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$:

| $d$ | fitted slope of $\log W_2$ against $\log n$ | $-1/d$ |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | $-0.193$ | $-0.200$ |
| 10 | $-0.106$ | $-0.100$ |
| 20 | $-0.065$ | $-0.050$ |

So a Wasserstein distance *estimated from samples* in high dimension is mostly
noise, however exactly you solve the transport problem. Solving the wrong problem
precisely does not help.

**Sliced Wasserstein** is the standard dodge: project both distributions onto a
random direction $\theta$, where the closed form applies, and average over
directions,

$$
SW_p^p(P,Q) = \int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} W_p^p\big(\theta_\# P,\ \theta_\# Q\big)\, d\theta .
$$

Each slice is a sort. It is a genuine metric, it is cheap, and it inherits the
better one-dimensional rate — at the cost of being a weaker comparison that can
be fooled by structure invisible to every projection.

## 6. Integral probability metrics, in general

Wasserstein and MMD are both instances of one construction. Given a class
$\mathcal{F}$ of real-valued **test functions**,

$$
d_{\mathcal{F}}(P,Q) \;=\; \sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}}
\Big| \mathbb{E}_{P}[f] - \mathbb{E}_{Q}[f] \Big| .
$$

Read it as a search for a **witness**: a single function on which the two
distributions disagree as loudly as possible. If no test function can tell them
apart, they are the same as far as $\mathcal{F}$ can see.

Everything depends on how rich $\mathcal{F}$ is, and the choice is a genuine
trade-off in both directions:

- $\mathcal{F}$ too **small** and the metric is blind — it will report zero for
  distributions that genuinely differ.
- $\mathcal{F}$ too **large** and the supremum cannot be estimated from finitely
  many samples — the empirical witness overfits, and the estimate is biased upward
  no matter how much data you have.

| Class $\mathcal{F}$ | Resulting IPM | Witness is |
|---|---|---|
| $\lVert f \rVert_{\mathrm{Lip}} \le 1$ | **Wasserstein-1** | a Lipschitz function — the WGAN critic |
| unit ball of an RKHS $\mathcal{H}$ | **MMD** | available in closed form (§7) |
| $\lVert f \rVert_\infty \le \tfrac12$ | **total variation** | an indicator of a set |
| bounded, with bounded derivatives | Dudley metric | a smooth bump |

Two structural remarks. First, **IPMs are symmetric and satisfy the triangle
inequality** whenever $\mathcal{F}$ is symmetric ($f \in \mathcal{F} \Rightarrow
-f \in \mathcal{F}$), so they are honest metrics — unlike KL. Second, and this is
the substantive contrast with §4, an IPM is defined through **expectations of
functions on the space**, so it knows how far apart points are. An
$f$-divergence is defined through a *ratio of densities at the same point*, so it
knows only how much the two disagree there, never how far anything had to move.
That single difference is what §8 is about.

**Total variation is the intersection.** It is an $f$-divergence
($f(t) = \tfrac12|t-1|$) *and* an IPM (bounded test functions) *and* a metric —
essentially the only member of both families, which is a good way to remember
that they are otherwise disjoint.

## 7. Maximum mean discrepancy: the IPM you can actually compute

Wasserstein's definition contains an infimum over couplings; the IPM form
contains a supremum over functions. Both are optimisation problems. **MMD is the
choice of $\mathcal{F}$ for which the optimisation can be solved in closed form**,
and that is essentially the whole reason it exists.

Take $\mathcal{F}$ to be the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space
$\mathcal{H}$ with kernel $k$. Define the **kernel mean embedding** of a
distribution,

$$
\mu_P \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{X \sim P}\big[\, k(X, \cdot)\,\big] \;\in\; \mathcal{H},
$$

a single point in $\mathcal{H}$ that summarises the whole distribution. The
reproducing property gives $\mathbb{E}_P[f] = \langle f, \mu_P\rangle$ for every
$f \in \mathcal{H}$, so

$$
\mathrm{MMD}(P,Q) = \sup_{\lVert f \rVert_{\mathcal{H}} \le 1}
\langle f, \mu_P - \mu_Q \rangle = \lVert \mu_P - \mu_Q \rVert_{\mathcal{H}} .
$$

The supremum is attained by the obvious witness, $f \propto \mu_P - \mu_Q$, and
the value is just a norm. Expanding it,

$$
\boxed{\;\mathrm{MMD}^2(P,Q) = \mathbb{E}\,k(X,X') - 2\,\mathbb{E}\,k(X,Y) + \mathbb{E}\,k(Y,Y')\;}
$$

with $X, X' \sim P$ and $Y, Y' \sim Q$ independent. **Three expectations of a
kernel — no densities, no couplings, no optimisation.** Replacing them by sample
averages (dropping diagonal terms) gives an unbiased estimator computable in
$O(n^2)$, or $O(n)$ with a linear-time variant.

**Does it separate distributions?** Only if the kernel is **characteristic**,
meaning $P \mapsto \mu_P$ is injective. The Gaussian RBF and Laplace kernels are;
a linear kernel is not — it embeds only the mean, so it cannot distinguish any two
distributions with the same mean. With a characteristic kernel,
$\mathrm{MMD}(P,Q) = 0 \iff P = Q$.

**A closed form to test against.** For $P = \mathcal{N}(a, I_d)$,
$Q = \mathcal{N}(b, I_d)$ and Gaussian kernel of bandwidth $s$,

$$
\mathrm{MMD}^2 = \frac{2\,s^d}{(2+s^2)^{d/2}}
\left(1 - \exp\!\Big(-\frac{\lVert a-b\rVert^2}{2(2+s^2)}\Big)\right).
$$

*(Checked: at $\lVert a - b\rVert = 1$ and $s = \sqrt{d}$, the formula gives
$0.1175$, $0.0328$, $0.0072$ for $d = 2, 10, 50$, and the sample estimator returns
$0.1214$, $0.0317$, $0.0071$.)*

### The headline property, and its asterisk

The MMD estimator converges at $n^{-1/2}$ **independently of the dimension** —
there is no $n^{-1/d}$ anywhere. Measured slopes of $\log|\hat{}-\text{truth}|$
against $\log n$: $-0.55$ at $d=2$, $-0.71$ at $d=10$, $-0.48$ at $d=50$. Against
Wasserstein's $n^{-1/d}$ this looks like a free lunch.

::: {.callout-warning}
## It is not a free lunch

Look again at the closed form above. For a *fixed* separation $\lVert a-b\rVert = 1$,
the population MMD itself falls with dimension — $0.1175$, $0.0328$, $0.0072$ at
$d = 2, 10, 50$. The **error** shrinks at $n^{-1/2}$ regardless of $d$, but the
**signal** you are trying to detect shrinks too. What matters for a test is the
ratio, and that still degrades.

So the honest statement is: MMD moves the curse from the *estimation rate* into
the *effect size*. It does not abolish it. It also depends on a bandwidth $s$ that
you must choose — the median heuristic (set $s$ to the median pairwise distance)
is the usual default and is a heuristic, not a theorem.
:::

MMD's real strengths are that it needs only samples, costs $O(n^2)$ with no inner
optimisation, is differentiable in the samples — hence usable directly as a
training loss, as in MMD-GAN — and comes with a clean two-sample test
(Gretton et al.), which is how one asks "did my generative model actually match
the data?" with a $p$-value attached.

### Choosing between them

| | $f$-divergence (KL, JS) | Wasserstein | MMD |
|---|---|---|---|
| Needs densities | yes | no | no |
| Sees geometry | no | yes | partly — through the kernel |
| Disjoint supports | saturates | degrades gracefully | degrades gracefully |
| Closed form in $d$ dims | Gaussians only | Gaussians only (Bures) | any kernel, from samples |
| Cost from $n$ samples | needs a density model | $O(n^3\log n)$, or $O(n^2)$ Sinkhorn | $O(n^2)$, no optimisation |
| Estimation rate | — | $n^{-1/d}$ | $n^{-1/2}$, but shrinking signal |
| A metric | no | yes | yes (characteristic kernel) |

## 8. Why the distinction is not pedantry: disjoint supports

Take $P$ uniform on $[0,1]$ and $Q$ uniform on $[d, d+1]$ — the same shape, shifted
by $d$. Watch what each measure reports as $d$ grows:

| shift $d$ | overlap | $\mathrm{KL}$ | JS | TV | $W_1$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 0.5 | $\infty$ | $< \log 2$ | 0.50 | 0.50 |
| 1.0 | 0 | $\infty$ | $\log 2$ | 1 | 1.00 |
| 2.0 | 0 | $\infty$ | $\log 2$ | 1 | 2.00 |
| 5.0 | 0 | $\infty$ | $\log 2$ | 1 | 5.00 |

Once the supports separate, every $f$-divergence **stops responding**. KL is
already infinite; JS is pinned at $\log 2$; TV is pinned at 1. They report "as
different as possible" and cannot distinguish a near miss from a wild one. Their
gradients with respect to $d$ are zero — so a model trained on them gets no signal
telling it which way to move.

$W_1$ reports $d$. It keeps growing, and its gradient points home.

::: {.callout-important}
## This is the WGAN argument

Arjovsky, Chintala and Bottou (2017) built Wasserstein GAN on exactly this
observation. A generator's output distribution is supported on a
low-dimensional manifold in a high-dimensional space — the manifold hypothesis of
[Measuring Things](./10-measuring-things.qmd) — and so is the data. Two such
manifolds generically intersect in a set of measure zero, so the supports are
*essentially disjoint from the start*, and JS (which the original GAN minimises at
an optimal discriminator) is pinned at $\log 2$ with vanishing gradient. Replacing
it with $W_1$, estimated through the Kantorovich–Rubinstein dual with a
Lipschitz-constrained critic, restores a usable gradient.

Notice that the same fact motivates diffusion models' use of noise, for the same
reason: convolving with a Gaussian makes the supports overlap, so the
ratio-based quantities become finite and informative again.
:::

## 9. The map: what is each model family minimising?

| Model | Objective, in divergence terms |
|---|---|
| **Maximum likelihood / normalizing flows** | forward $\mathrm{KL}(p_{\text{data}}\|p_\theta)$, exactly (§3) |
| **VAE / autoencoders** | maximise the ELBO $= \log p(x) - \mathrm{KL}(q(z\mid x)\,\|\,p(z\mid x))$; the trainable form contains an explicit $\mathrm{KL}(q(z\mid x)\,\|\,p(z))$ against the prior |
| **Original GAN** | at an optimal discriminator, Jensen–Shannon — an $f$-divergence |
| **$f$-GAN** | any $f$-divergence, via its variational (Fenchel) representation |
| **WGAN** | $W_1$ — an IPM, deliberately not an $f$-divergence |
| **MMD nets** | MMD — also an IPM |
| **Diffusion models** | a variational bound that decomposes into a sum of KLs between Gaussians, each with the closed form of §2; equivalently, denoising score matching |

Read down that column and the structure the whole field shares comes into view:
**every generative model is minimising some divergence between the data
distribution and the model's**. What distinguishes the families is *which*
divergence, and — because it is usually not computable directly — *how they get at
it*: a bound (VAE), a learned dual (GAN, WGAN), a closed form after adding noise
(diffusion), or exactly (flows).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key takeaway

In one dimension everything is a norm of the CDF gap: sup gives
Kolmogorov–Smirnov, $L^1$ gives Wasserstein-1 which is a transport cost, $L^2$
gives Cramér–von Mises. Beyond one dimension the CDF fails and two families take
over. **$f$-divergences** — KL, JS, TV, $\chi^2$ — compare densities through their
pointwise ratio and are blind to distance, which makes them infinite or saturated
when supports disagree. **Integral probability metrics** — Wasserstein, MMD —
compare through test functions and do see distance, which is why they keep working
when the supports come apart. Total variation is the one member of both.
:::

## Exercises

1. Show that in one dimension the monotone coupling is optimal for any convex
   cost, and deduce $W_1 = \int|F-G|$.
2. Verify the Bures–Wasserstein formula for two diagonal Gaussians directly, and
   confirm it reduces to $\lVert C_1^{1/2}-C_2^{1/2}\rVert_F^2$ plus the squared
   mean gap.
3. Why does the quantile construction fail in $\mathbb{R}^2$? Give two
   distributions for which several distinct plans have the same cost.
4. Brenier's map is $\nabla\varphi$ with $\varphi$ convex. What is $\varphi$ in
   one dimension, and why is convexity the right generalisation of monotonicity?
5. Take $P=\mathcal{N}(0,I_d)$ and $Q=\mathcal{N}(\delta e_1, I_d)$. Compute $W_2$
   exactly. Now compute the sliced Wasserstein distance and compare.
6. Show any IPM with a symmetric $\mathcal{F}$ obeys the triangle inequality.
7. Show a linear kernel is not characteristic by exhibiting $P \ne Q$ with
   $\mathrm{MMD}=0$.
8. Derive the MMD expansion $\mathbb{E}k(X,X') - 2\mathbb{E}k(X,Y) +
   \mathbb{E}k(Y,Y')$ from $\lVert \mu_P-\mu_Q\rVert^2_{\mathcal{H}}$.
9. Using the Gaussian-kernel closed form, compute $\mathrm{MMD}^2$ at
   $\lVert a-b\rVert=1$, $s=\sqrt{d}$, for $d=2,10,50$. Explain why the
   dimension-free $n^{-1/2}$ rate is nevertheless not a free lunch.
10. Why is the diagonal dropped from the MMD estimator? What happens if you
    keep it?

### Earlier exercises

1. For $P = \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and $Q = \mathcal{N}(\mu,1)$, show the KS statistic
   is $2\Phi(\mu/2)-1$ by finding where the CDF gap is maximised. Evaluate at
   $\mu = 1$ and $\mu = 4$ and comment on the saturation.
2. Show $\int|F-G|\,dx = W_1$ for these two Gaussians equals exactly $|\mu|$, and
   explain why it does not saturate.
3. Derive $\mathrm{KL}(\mathcal{N}(\mu_1,\sigma^2)\|\mathcal{N}(\mu_2,\sigma^2))
   = (\mu_1-\mu_2)^2/2\sigma^2$ from the general Gaussian formula, and say why this
   makes diffusion training objectives reduce to squared errors.
4. Prove $\mathrm{KL} \ge 0$ using Jensen, and identify exactly where equality
   requires $p = q$ almost everywhere.
5. Give two distributions with $\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)$ finite and
   $\mathrm{KL}(q\|p) = \infty$. *(Hint: make one support strictly contain the other.)*
6. Verify that $f(t) = t\log t$ gives KL and $f(t) = \tfrac12|t-1|$ gives total
   variation in the definition $D_f = \int q f(p/q)$.
7. Explain in your own words why no $f$-divergence can distinguish "$Q$ is just
   beside $P$" from "$Q$ is a mile away", once the supports are disjoint. Then say
   what an IPM does differently.
8. For $P$ uniform on $[0,1]$ and $Q$ uniform on $[d,d+1]$ with $d > 1$, compute
   $W_1$, TV and JS. Which of the three would give a usable training gradient in
   $d$, and why?
